question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

CONNOISSEUR
option_4: Amateur
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Expert judge.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A connoisseur is a person with expert knowledge and refined taste, especially in matters of art, food, wine or music. (पारखी, रसज्ञ)
◦ Example: Only a connoisseur could tell the two vintages apart.

 

• Expert judge captures precisely this sense — someone whose discrimination is authoritative because it rests on long experience.

 

• The word is borrowed from French, from connaître, "to know" — the same root as cognisance and recognise. Note the tricky spelling: CON + NOIS + SEUR, with a double "n".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Novice (नवसिखिया): a beginner with no experience — the opposite of a connoisseur.

 

• Option 2: Apprentice (शिक्षु): a learner working under a skilled master — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Amateur (शौकिया): one who pursues an activity for pleasure rather than as a profession, and often without expertise — again an antonym in this context.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of connoisseur: aficionado, cognoscente, savant, epicure and gourmet (of food specifically).

 

• Person-nouns of this kind are a standing SSC favourite: bibliophile (book-lover), philatelist (stamp collector), numismatist (coin collector), oenophile (wine-lover) and audiophile (one devoted to sound quality).

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To have an axe to grind
option_1: To have a private or selfish motive behind one's actions
option_2: To sharpen one's skills through constant practice
option_3: To nurse a grudge in silence for many years
option_4: To perform heavy physical labour without complaint
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To have a private or selfish motive behind one's actions.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To have an axe to grind" means to have a personal, and usually concealed, interest in a matter, so that one's apparent concern for a cause is really self-serving. (अपना उल्लू सीधा करना)
◦ Example: He supported the transfer policy so warmly that everyone suspected he had an axe to grind.

 

• The phrase is traced to an anecdote in which a stranger flatters a boy into turning a heavy grindstone for him, and walks off without a word of thanks once his own axe is sharpened. The flattery was a means, not a courtesy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the idiom literally as self-improvement, which is the commonest trap here.

 

• Option 3 describes a lasting resentment, for which the idiom would be "to bear a grudge" or "to nurse a grievance".

 

• Option 4 describes hard work, nearer to "to put one's shoulder to the wheel".

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of hidden motive frequently asked in SSC: "To have an ulterior motive", "A wolf in sheep's clothing", "To play a double game" and "To feather one's own nest" (to enrich oneself while holding a position of trust).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

PELLUCID
option_4: Obscure
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Obscure.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pellucid (adjective) means admirably clear — either physically transparent, as of water and glass, or, of speech and writing, easy to understand. (स्फटिक-सा स्वच्छ, स्पष्ट)
◦ Example: Her pellucid explanation of the rule left no room for doubt.

 

• Its true opposite is obscure — not clearly expressed; difficult to understand, or hidden from view. (अस्पष्ट, दुर्बोध)
◦ Example: The clause was so obscure that even the drafters disagreed about it.

 

• The word is built from Latin per (through) + lucere (to shine) — literally shining through. The same root gives lucid, translucent and elucidate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Transparent (पारदर्शी): allowing light to pass through so that objects behind are clearly seen — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Lucid (स्पष्ट): clearly expressed and easily understood — also a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Limpid (निर्मल): clear and untroubled, used of water, eyes and prose — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of pellucid: opaque, turbid, murky, abstruse, unintelligible.

 

• Useful contrast for SSC: transparent (see through clearly), translucent (light passes but images blur) and opaque (no light passes at all).

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
option_4: Hypocrisy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Superintendant.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Superintendent" — a person who directs or manages an organisation, department or office. (अधीक्षक)
◦ Example: The Superintendent of Police visited the examination centre.

 

• Spelling key: SUPER + IN + TEND + ENT. The word ends in "-ent", not "-ant", because it belongs with tend, attend, superintend — all of which give -endent/-endant forms ending in -ent when they name an office holder.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Idiosyncrasy (व्यक्तिगत विशेषता) — correctly spelt; note the ending "-crasy", not "-cracy".

 

• Option 2: Paraphernalia (साज-सामान) — correctly spelt; note the "pher" in the middle.

 

• Option 4: Hypocrisy (पाखंड) — correctly spelt; the adjective is hypocritical and the noun for the person is hypocrite.

 

NOTE

 

• The -ent / -ant distinction is tested repeatedly. Take -ent: superintendent, independent, correspondent, persistent, existent, competent. Take -ant: attendant, defendant, descendant, assistant, relevant, significant.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the cellular process by which solid particles are engulfed and ingested.
option_4: Phagocitosis
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Phagocytosis.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Phagocytosis" is the process by which a cell engulfs a solid particle — such as a bacterium or cell debris — and encloses it within a vesicle for digestion. It is a key part of the body's immune defence. (कोशिका द्वारा कणों को निगलना)
◦ Example: White blood cells destroy invading bacteria by phagocytosis.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: PHAGO (to eat) + CYTO (cell) + OSIS (process or condition). The same roots appear in phagocyte, cytoplasm and osmosis.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Phagositosis" — incorrect; the root is "cyto", spelt with c and y.

 

• Option 3: "Phagocytosys" — incorrect; the suffix is "-osis", not "-osys".

 

• Option 4: "Phagocitosis" — incorrect; "i" has been substituted for the "y" of cyto.

 

NOTE

 

• Related processes worth distinguishing: pinocytosis (the cell takes in liquid), exocytosis (material is expelled from the cell) and endocytosis (the general term for taking material in).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A formal agreement between opposing sides to stop fighting for a time'
option_4: Armistice
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Armistice.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An armistice is a formal agreement between warring parties to suspend hostilities, usually while terms of peace are being negotiated. It stops the fighting; it does not by itself end the war. (युद्धविराम)
◦ Example: The armistice of 11 November 1918 brought the fighting of the First World War to an end.

 

• The word comes from Latin arma (arms) + -stitium (a stopping) — literally a standing still of arms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Treaty (संधि): a formal agreement between states, which concludes a war or settles some other matter permanently.

 

• Option 2: Accord (समझौता): a general term for an agreement or settlement, with no necessary link to warfare.

 

• Option 3: Detente (तनाव में कमी): an easing of strained relations between countries, and not a formal agreement at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Related one-word substitutes: Truce (an informal or temporary halt in fighting), Ceasefire (an order to stop firing), Amnesty (a general pardon for political offences) and Reparations (compensation paid by a defeated state).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The instructions were couched in ___ technical language that most of the applicants gave up halfway.
option_4: very
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. such.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The rule turns on what follows the blank:

◦ "such" + (adjective) + NOUN + that — such technical language that…
◦ "so" + ADJECTIVE/ADVERB (alone) + that — so technical that…

 

• Here the blank is followed by the adjective technical and the noun "language", so "such" is required. Had the sentence read The instructions were ___ technical that most applicants gave up, the answer would have been so.

◦ Example: It was such a difficult paper that half the candidates left early. / The paper was so difficult that half the candidates left early.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: so — cannot be used directly before a noun phrase.

 

• Option 3: too — pairs with an infinitive, not with that: too technical to follow.

 

• Option 4: very — simply intensifies; it does not introduce a that-clause of result.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the three result structures apart: so … that, such … that, and too … to. Note also that too carries a negative sense — too weak to walk means he cannot walk.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The scheme was announced with great fanfare in March; ___, not a single beneficiary had been enrolled by December.
option_4: consequently
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. however.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The two clauses stand in contrast: a grand announcement in one, and nothing achieved in the other. The connector must therefore express opposition, and "however" is the only such option.

◦ Example: The road was widened last year; however, the traffic has grown worse.

 

• Note the punctuation, which SSC also tests: a conjunctive adverb such as however joining two independent clauses takes a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: therefore, Option 2: accordingly and Option 4: consequently all express result, which would require the second clause to follow logically from the first. Here it contradicts it.

 

• This is a common SSC design: three connectors of one relation and one of another. Decide the relation between the clauses first, then look at the options.

 

NOTE

 

• Group the connectors by function: Contrast — however, nevertheless, nonetheless, yet, on the contrary, conversely. Result — therefore, hence, thus, consequently, accordingly. Addition — moreover, furthermore, besides, in addition. Example — for instance, namely, that is.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The dispute over grazing rights, left unattended for months, soon ___ into a full-blown agitation.
option_4: aggravated
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. escalated.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Escalate" means to increase rapidly in intensity, scale or seriousness, and it is the standard verb for a conflict growing into something larger. It is followed by "into", exactly as the sentence requires. (बढ़ जाना, उग्र रूप लेना)
◦ Example: A quarrel between two shopkeepers escalated into a market-wide strike.

 

• The clue words are "left unattended for months" and "full-blown", both of which point to a small matter growing into a large one.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: elevate (ऊँचा उठाना): to raise in height, rank or status — he was elevated to the Bench. It is not used of conflicts.

 

• Option 3: accelerate (गति बढ़ाना): to increase speed, not seriousness.

 

• Option 4: aggravate (गंभीर बनाना): to make an existing bad situation worse. It takes a direct object — the delay aggravated the dispute — and is never followed by into.

 

NOTE

 

• Collocations worth memorising: escalate into a crisis; degenerate into chaos; culminate in a settlement; result in a loss; snowball into a controversy.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The revised syllabus is (1)/ more simpler than the previous one (2)/ and can be covered comfortably (3)/ within a single academic year. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is a double comparative. The word "simpler" is already the comparative form of simple, so placing "more" before it repeats the comparison.

◦ Corrected sentence: The revised syllabus is simpler than the previous one and can be covered comfortably within a single academic year.

 

• The rule: an adjective takes either the -er/-est ending or more/most, never both. Short adjectives normally take the ending (simple – simpler – simplest), while longer ones take more/most (difficult – more difficult – most difficult).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the singular subject syllabus agrees with is.

 

• Part (3) is correct — the modal passive can be covered is properly formed.

 

• Part (4) is correct — within is the right preposition for a period inside which something is completed.

 

NOTE

 

• The same error appears as a double superlative: the most easiest way should be the easiest way.

 

• Some adjectives are absolute and admit no comparison at all: unique, perfect, complete, universal, supreme, eternal. More unique and most perfect are therefore both wrong.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The manager stated (1)/ that he had not received (2)/ no intimation about the change in schedule (3)/ from the head office. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence contains a double negative. The clause already carries the negative "had not received" in part (2), so adding "no intimation" in part (3) negates the statement twice.

 

• In standard English two negatives in the same clause cancel each other out, producing the opposite of the intended meaning. Only one negative word may be used.

◦ Corrected sentence: The manager stated that he had not received any intimation about the change in schedule from the head office.
◦ Or: … that he had received no intimation about the change in schedule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — stated that is a well-formed reporting structure.

 

• Part (2) is correct in itself; the past perfect suits a fact existing before the statement was made.

 

• Part (4) is correct — from is the right preposition for the source of a communication.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember that hardly, scarcely, barely, seldom, rarely, neither, nor and lest are already negative, and must never be paired with another negative:
◦ I can hardly see anything — not hardly see nothing.
◦ Take care lest you fall — not lest you should not fall.
◦ Unless you hurry… — not unless you do not hurry.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The engineers had inspected the bridge before the monsoon set in.
option_1: The bridge had been inspected by the engineers before the monsoon set in.
option_2: The bridge was inspected by the engineers before the monsoon set in.
option_3: The bridge has been inspected by the engineers before the monsoon set in.
option_4: The bridge had inspected by the engineers before the monsoon set in.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The bridge had been inspected by the engineers before the monsoon set in.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Past Perfect Tense — structure: Subject + had + V3.

 

• The passive of the past perfect is formed as: Object + had been + V3 + by + Subject.

◦ Active: The engineers had inspected the bridge.
◦ Passive: The bridge had been inspected by the engineers.

 

• "Had been" does not change with number — it is the same for singular and plural subjects, unlike was/were or has/have been.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses "was inspected", the passive of the simple past, which loses the sense of one action completed before another.

 

• Option 3 uses "has been inspected", the passive of the present perfect, wrongly linking the action to the present.

 

• Option 4 omits "been", leaving had inspected — an active form with a passive agent, which is ungrammatical.

 

NOTE

 

• When two past actions are reported, the earlier one takes the past perfect and the later one the simple past. Here the inspection (had been inspected) precedes the monsoon (set in), and that relationship must survive the conversion.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The results will be announced by the board next Monday.
option_1: The board announces the results next Monday.
option_2: The board announced the results next Monday.
option_3: The board will announce the results next Monday.
option_4: The results will announce by the board next Monday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The board will announce the results next Monday.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Simple Future Passive — structure: will be + V3. Its active counterpart is will + V1.

◦ Passive: The results will be announced by the board.
◦ Active: The board will announce the results.

 

• In the conversion the agent after "by" (the board) becomes the subject, the original subject (the results) becomes the object, and the future tense is preserved — confirmed here by the time expression next Monday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts to the simple present, which clashes with next Monday.

 

• Option 2 shifts to the simple past, placing a future event in the past.

 

• Option 4 is neither properly active nor passive — will announce is active in form but keeps by the board, so the results appear to be doing the announcing.

 

NOTE

 

• The time expression in the sentence is the quickest check on tense during voice conversion. Yesterday, last week, in 1947 fix the past; now, at present the present; tomorrow, next Monday, shortly the future.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The principal addressed the assembly on the first morning of the session.
option_1: The principal signed the transfer certificate herself.
option_2: She met the principal outside the staff room.
option_3: The principal of the college inaugurated the seminar.
option_4: He resigned on a matter of principle rather than of pay.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He resigned on a matter of principle rather than of pay.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Principal is a noun meaning the head of a school or college, or the original sum of money in a loan; as an adjective it means chief or most important.
• Principle is a noun only, meaning a rule of conduct, a fundamental truth or a moral standard. The two are pronounced alike, so "principle" is the homophone required here.

◦ Example: The scheme rests on the principle that no candidate should pay a fee twice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all reuse the same spelling "principal" in the sense of the head of an institution, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: the principal is your pal at school; a principle is a rule — both end in -le.

 

• Note also that principle has no adjective form. A principled stand uses the past participle, not an adjective from principal.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

A language disappears somewhere in the world roughly every fortnight. The figure is repeated so often that it has lost its power to unsettle, and the loss is commonly explained away as a natural consequence of progress. Speakers of small languages, the argument runs, abandon them voluntarily in favour of larger ones that open doors to schooling, employment and government. Nobody is coerced; a rational calculation is simply being made.

 

The premise is largely true and the conclusion largely false. The calculation is real, but it is rarely free. A child corrected for speaking her mother tongue in a classroom, a farmer whose land records exist only in the state language, an advertisement that presumes fluency in a third — none of these is compulsion in the legal sense, yet together they leave a household with one sensible option. What looks like preference is often the shape that pressure takes when it is applied slowly.

 

What is actually lost when a language goes is harder to state than it seems. It is not the vocabulary; words can be recorded. It is the categories that the vocabulary carries — a fisherman's forty terms for the states of a tidal creek, a herder's grammar of animal age and temperament, the names of plants whose uses no botanist has yet catalogued. Such knowledge is not so much translated as abandoned, because the language that carried it was the only place it had ever been kept.

 

None of this argues for freezing communities in place. A language survives because it is spoken, not because it is admired, and a speaker who wants a wider world is entitled to it. What the argument does suggest is that the choice is usually posed as an either-or when it need not be. Children raised with two languages surrender nothing. It is monolingualism, not multilingualism, that is the historical anomaly.

 

According to the passage, what is the explanation usually offered for the disappearance of languages?
option_1: That governments deliberately suppress smaller languages
option_2: That speakers voluntarily switch to larger languages offering wider opportunity
option_3: That smaller languages lack the vocabulary needed for modern life
option_4: That written records of such languages were never maintained
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That speakers voluntarily switch to larger languages offering wider opportunity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first paragraph reports the standard explanation: speakers of small languages abandon them voluntarily in favour of larger ones that open doors to schooling, employment and government, so that nobody is coerced and a rational calculation is simply being made.

 

• Note that the author is reporting this view, not endorsing it — the next paragraph opens by calling the conclusion largely false. The question, however, asks only what the usual explanation is.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 states the opposite of the usual explanation, which insists that nobody is coerced.

 

• Option 3 is contradicted by the third paragraph, which describes small languages as carrying knowledge richer than the larger ones possess.

 

• Option 4 raises written records, which the passage mentions only to say that recording words is not what preserves a language.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish carefully between what an author reports and what an author believes. SSC frequently sets one question on the view being criticised and another on the criticism itself.

Why does the author say that the calculation is "rarely free"?
option_1: Because switching languages involves a heavy financial cost
option_2: Because most speakers are legally forbidden to use their mother tongue
option_3: Because larger languages are harder to learn than smaller ones
option_4: Because accumulated everyday pressures leave a household only one sensible option
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Because accumulated everyday pressures leave a household only one sensible option.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The author lists three ordinary circumstances — a child corrected in class, land records kept only in the state language, an advertisement presuming a third language — and concedes that none of these is compulsion in the legal sense.

 

• The point is that their combined effect is decisive: together they leave a household with one sensible option. The choice remains a choice in form, but not in substance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces a financial cost that the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 2 is expressly denied — the author states that none of the pressures amounts to legal compulsion.

 

• Option 3 raises comparative difficulty of learning, a point absent from the text.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage lists several examples and then draws a single conclusion, the conclusion is the answer, not any one example. Here the conclusion is the clause beginning "yet together they …".

According to the author, what is chiefly lost when a language dies?
option_1: The categories of knowledge that its vocabulary carried
option_2: The literature that was written in it
option_3: The vocabulary itself, which cannot be recorded
option_4: The community's sense of political identity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The categories of knowledge that its vocabulary carried.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph is explicit: what is lost is not the vocabulary, since words can be recorded. It is the categories that the vocabulary carries.

 

• The author illustrates this with three examples — a fisherman's forty terms for the states of a tidal creek, a herder's grammar of animal age and temperament, and the names of plants whose uses no botanist has yet catalogued. Such knowledge is not so much translated as abandoned.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 mentions literature, which this passage does not discuss at all.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the passage directly — the author says words can be recorded.

 

• Option 4 introduces political identity, a theme the author avoids.

 

NOTE

 

• The construction "It is not X. It is Y." is a standard SSC trap: one option is always built from X, the item the author has just ruled out. Read both sentences before choosing.

What is actually lost when a language goes is harder to state than it seems. It is not the vocabulary; words can be recorded. It is the categories that the vocabulary carries — a fisherman's forty terms for the states of a tidal creek, a herder's grammar of animal age and temperament, the names of plants whose uses no botanist has yet catalogued. Such knowledge is not so much translated as abandoned, because the language that carried it was the only place it had ever been kept.

 

None of this argues for freezing communities in place. A language survives because it is spoken, not because it is admired, and a speaker who wants a wider world is entitled to it. What the argument does suggest is that the choice is usually posed as an either-or when it need not be. Children raised with two languages surrender nothing. It is monolingualism, not multilingualism, that is the historical anomaly.

 

What is implied by the phrase "the shape that pressure takes when it is applied slowly"?
option_1: That pressure applied gradually is easier for communities to resist
option_2: That governments prefer gradual reform to sudden change
option_3: That coercion which is not legally recognisable can still be decisive
option_4: That language change always takes several generations to complete
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. That coercion which is not legally recognisable can still be decisive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase closes the author's argument that what looks like preference is in fact the result of pressure. Because the pressure is spread across years and across ordinary institutions — the classroom, the land office, the job market — it never appears as an order that anyone could point to.

 

• The author's claim is therefore about form versus effect: the compulsion is invisible in form (nothing illegal has occurred) but complete in effect (only one option remains).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the sense — slow pressure is presented as harder to resist, precisely because it is hard to identify.

 

• Option 2 turns the phrase into a comment on government policy, which the passage does not make.

 

• Option 4 treats the phrase as a statement about time-scale only, missing the point about coercion.

 

NOTE

 

• For implication questions, ask what the author is arguing against. Here the target is the claim that nobody is coerced, so the answer must be about coercion of a kind that the legal test would miss.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

A language disappears somewhere in the world roughly every fortnight. The figure is repeated so often that it has lost its power to unsettle, and the loss is commonly explained away as a natural consequence of progress. Speakers of small languages, the argument runs, abandon them voluntarily in favour of larger ones that open doors to schooling, employment and government. Nobody is coerced; a rational calculation is simply being made.

 

The premise is largely true and the conclusion largely false. The calculation is real, but it is rarely free. A child corrected for speaking her mother tongue in a classroom, a farmer whose land records exist only in the state language, an advertisement that presumes fluency in a third — none of these is compulsion in the legal sense, yet together they leave a household with one sensible option. What looks like preference is often the shape that pressure takes when it is applied slowly.

 

What is actually lost when a language goes is harder to state than it seems. It is not the vocabulary; words can be recorded. It is the categories that the vocabulary carries — a fisherman's forty terms for the states of a tidal creek, a herder's grammar of animal age and temperament, the names of plants whose uses no botanist has yet catalogued. Such knowledge is not so much translated as abandoned, because the language that carried it was the only place it had ever been kept.

 

None of this argues for freezing communities in place. A language survives because it is spoken, not because it is admired, and a speaker who wants a wider world is entitled to it. What the argument does suggest is that the choice is usually posed as an either-or when it need not be. Children raised with two languages surrender nothing. It is monolingualism, not multilingualism, that is the historical anomaly.

 

What does the word "anomaly" in the last line of the passage most nearly mean?
option_2: Something that departs from what is normal or expected
option_4: An advantage enjoyed by a few
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Something that departs from what is normal or expected.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An anomaly is something that deviates from what is standard, normal or expected — an irregularity or exception. (विसंगति, अपवाद)
◦ Example: A rainless July is an anomaly in this region.

 

• The context makes the sense plain. The author writes that it is monolingualism, not multilingualism, that is the historical anomaly — that is, speaking only one language is the exception in human history, not the rule. This overturns the assumption on which the whole "either-or" argument rests.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the opposite — an anomaly is precisely what is not usual.

 

• Option 3 describes a trend, not a deviation.

 

• Option 4 confuses an anomaly with a privilege.

 

NOTE

 

• Synonyms of anomaly: aberration, irregularity, deviation, incongruity, oddity. Antonyms: norm, regularity, standard, conformity.

 

• For word-meaning-in-context questions, always test the candidate meaning by substituting it in the sentence. Here "exception" fits and "custom" plainly does not.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

This is one of the best film I have seen this year.
option_4: most best films
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. best films.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The structure "one of the + superlative" must be followed by a plural noun, because one of selects a single item out of a group.

◦ Corrected sentence: This is one of the best films I have seen this year.
◦ Example: He is one of the finest players in the league.

 

• Test it by rearranging: Of the best films I have seen this year, this is one. The plural becomes obvious.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "better film" uses the comparative, which cannot follow one of the, and keeps the noun singular.

 

• Option 3: "best of film" is not an English structure.

 

• Option 4: "most best films" is a double superlative — best is already the superlative of good.

 

NOTE

 

• Although the noun after one of the is plural, the main verb stays singular, because the subject is one: One of the best films is playing at the multiplex.

 

• Contrast the relative clause: This is one of the best films that have been made this decade — there the verb follows films, not one.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The reason for his failure is because he did not revise the prescribed syllabus.
option_4: is due to he did not
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. is that he did not.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The construction "The reason … is because" is redundant, since reason and because both express cause. The noun reason must be completed by a noun clause introduced by "that".

◦ Corrected sentence: The reason for his failure is that he did not revise the prescribed syllabus.
◦ Or, more simply: He failed because he did not revise the prescribed syllabus.

 

• The same objection applies to "The reason is due to" and "The reason why … is because".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original redundancy.

 

• Option 2 corrects nothing and also shifts the tense to the past without cause.

 

• Option 4: "is due to he did not" is ungrammatical — due to is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or gerund, as in due to his failure to revise.

 

NOTE

 

• Other redundancies regularly tested by SSC: return back, repeat again, revert back, cooperate together, join together, final conclusion, free gift, past history, new innovation and advance planning.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He says, "I am busy with the audit today."
option_1: He says that he was busy with the audit that day.
option_2: He says that he is busy with the audit today.
option_3: He said that he was busy with the audit that day.
option_4: He says that he had been busy with the audit today.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He says that he is busy with the audit today.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The backshifting of tenses applies only when the reporting verb is in the past tense. Here the reporting verb is "says", which is in the present tense, so:

◦ the tense of the reported clause does not change — am becomes is only because the pronoun changes;
◦ the time and place words do not change — today stays today, not that day;
◦ only the pronoun changes, from I to he.

 

• The same rule applies when the reporting verb is in the present perfect (has said) or the future (will say).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 backshifts the tense and the time word although the reporting verb is present.

 

• Option 3 changes the reporting verb itself from says to said, which is not permitted — the reporting verb is given and must be retained.

 

• Option 4 introduces the past perfect, which has no basis in the original.

 

NOTE

 

• Summary of the rule: past reporting verb → backshift everything; present or future reporting verb → change only the pronouns. This single distinction settles a large share of SSC narration questions.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

He proposed to his colleagues that they should go for a walk after the meeting.
option_1: "We should go for a walk after the meeting," he said.
option_2: "Shall we go for a walk after the meeting?" he asked.
option_3: "Go for a walk after the meeting," he said.
option_4: "Let us go for a walk after the meeting," he said.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. "Let us go for a walk after the meeting," he said.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb "proposed … that they should" is the standard indirect form of a sentence beginning with "Let us", which expresses a proposal or suggestion made to the listeners.

 

• Restoring the direct speech reverses the rules:

◦ "proposed/suggested that … should" → "Let us …"
◦ The pronoun "they" → "us", since the speaker includes himself.
◦ The reporting verb becomes the neutral "said", and the words are enclosed in inverted commas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps should inside the quotation, turning a proposal into a statement of obligation.

 

• Option 2 makes it a question, whose indirect form would begin asked whether they should ….

 

• Option 3 is a plain imperative addressed to others and excludes the speaker; its indirect form would be told them to go for a walk.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the two "let" structures apart:
◦ "Let us" as a proposal → suggested/proposed that we should…
◦ "Let me / Let him" as a request for permission → requested that he might be allowed to…

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. For eleven years the primary school at Kotra had held its classes under a tamarind tree.

 

A. He measured the plot that evening and prepared a costing for a two-room shed.

 

B. The file, forwarded with his note attached, was cleared in under a month.

 

C. A junior engineer on transfer stopped one afternoon to ask why the children were sitting outside.

 

D. The estimate came to less than the district office was spending each year on whitewash.

 

S2. Kotra's children have had a roof over them since the following monsoon.
option_4: A-D-C-B
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. C-A-D-B.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – C – A – D – B – S2. The paragraph follows a situation → trigger → action → finding → outcome order.

 

• S1 states the situation — eleven years of classes under a tree.

◦ C supplies the trigger: the engineer's question. It must come first among the jumbled sentences, because "He" in A can refer to nobody else.
◦ A is his action — measuring the plot and preparing a costing.
◦ D reports the finding, and the words "The estimate" point directly back to the costing prepared in A.
◦ B gives the outcome — the file cleared in under a month — and leads into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-C-D-B) opens with "He" before the engineer has been introduced.

 

• Option 3 (C-D-A-B) mentions "The estimate" before any costing has been prepared.

 

• Option 4 (A-D-C-B) repeats both errors at once.

 

NOTE

 

• Two tests decide this question: the pronoun test (He in A requires C before it) and the definite-article test (The estimate in D requires the costing in A before it). Whenever a sentence opens with the + a noun not yet mentioned, it cannot come first.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The tomato is so central to Indian cooking that its absence from older recipes surprises most people.

 

A. For nearly three hundred years afterwards it was grown chiefly as a curiosity in colonial gardens.

 

B. It reached the subcontinent only in the sixteenth century, carried by Portuguese ships from the Americas.

 

C. Only in the late nineteenth century did it move out of those gardens and into ordinary kitchens.

 

D. Sourness in Indian cooking had until then come from tamarind, kokum, raw mango and fermented rice water.

 

S2. Few dishes that now seem timeless are much older than a hundred and fifty years in their present form.
option_4: A-B-D-C
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2. The paragraph moves in chronological order: arrival → what preceded it → slow adoption → final acceptance.

 

• S1 raises the puzzle — a supposedly essential ingredient is missing from older recipes.

◦ B answers it with the date of arrival, the sixteenth century. It must come first, since every other sentence is dated in relation to it.
◦ D follows B because "until then" can only refer to the moment of arrival just established, and it explains what Indian cooks used instead.
◦ A carries the story forward — "for nearly three hundred years afterwards" again measures from the arrival in B.
◦ C must follow A, because "those gardens" refers to the colonial gardens named there.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-A-D-C) separates until then in D from the date it depends on.

 

• Option 2 (D-B-A-C) opens with "until then", which has no antecedent at the start.

 

• Option 4 (A-B-D-C) begins with afterwards before anything has been dated.

 

NOTE

 

• In a chronological paragraph, look for time anchors — a century, a date, a decade — and for expressions that depend on one: until then, afterwards, by that time, only later. The anchor always comes first, and the dependent expressions follow in order.
